issues.legal_issue: A statutory purchase by a tenant vests ownership in the tenant and ends the landlord-tenant relationship, leaving the former landlord unable to pass title to others.
material_facts: The tenant held the agricultural land as a tenant on the statutory purchase date.
The landlord was alive and was not subject to a disability that postponed the statutory purchase.
The landlord later bequeathed the land, and the legatee and subsequent transferees claimed title through that bequest.
issues.conclusion: The tenant became the owner by operation of law on the statutory purchase date, ending the landlord-tenant relationship. The landlord and persons claiming through the landlord thereafter had no ownership title to transfer.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 32 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, a qualifying tenant became the deemed purchaser on the statutory date. The landlord's title was extinguished and title vested simultaneously in the tenant, without any act of transfer between the parties. The Court followed the Constitution Bench decision in Sri Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay, which held that the landlord's title passes to the tenant on the tillers' day, subject to the tenant's failure to appear, refusal to purchase, or default in payment of the price determined by the Tribunal.

predicates.agrarian_tenancy_purchase_case: The dispute concerns a statutory purchase of agricultural land by a tenant.
predicates.tenant_was_tenant_on_effective_date: The person claiming through the tenant held the land as a tenant on the date when the statutory purchase took effect.
predicates.landlord_had_no_purchase_postponing_disa: The landlord was not in a category of disability that postponed the statutory purchase.

issues.definition: When the case concerns a statutory tenant purchase, the tenant held the land on the effective date, and the landlord had no postponing disability, the tenant becomes the owner and the landlord-tenant relationship ends.

issues.legal_issue: Proceedings that assume a statutory purchase was postponed because a later recorded owner was a minor are nullities when the tenant had already become the owner, and their nullity may be raised in later proceedings.
material_facts: The tenant had become the owner before the landlord died and before the land was recorded in the name of a minor legatee.
Tribunal proceedings later treated the minor legatee's status as a reason to postpone the purchase.
Other proceedings proceeded on the assumption that the landlord-tenant relationship still existed.
Later authorities examined the tenant's status and treated the earlier proceedings as void.
issues.conclusion: The later proceedings were without jurisdiction and nullities, not merely erroneous orders, and their nullity could be raised in subsequent proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 32 and 32F of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, read together, postpone compulsory purchase only where the landlord had a specified disability on the relevant statutory date; the later status of a person claiming through the landlord does not alter a purchase already completed. A tribunal of limited jurisdiction that assumes jurisdiction on an incorrect jurisdictional fact, while ignoring the legal status created by statute, makes a null order that may be challenged collaterally.

predicates.tenant_purchase_proceeding_after_ownersh: A proceeding concerning statutory purchase was brought after the tenant had already acquired ownership.
predicates.tenant_already_owned_land: The tenant had become the owner before the proceeding began.
predicates.tribunal_assumed_purchase_was_postponed_: The tribunal treated a later claimant's status as a reason that the tenant's purchase had not yet taken effect.

issues.definition: If a purchase proceeding is brought after the tenant already owns the land and the tribunal assumes postponement because of a later claimant's status, the proceeding is a nullity that may be challenged later.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant's statement agreeing to surrender possession, made without knowledge of the ownership already acquired by operation of law, does not estop the tenant's successor from asserting that ownership or entitle the former landlord to possession.
material_facts: After becoming the statutory owner, the tenant stated in a possession proceeding that he was old, could not cultivate the land personally, and had no objection to handing over possession.
The tenant's son also made a statement concerning his lack of title during his father's lifetime.
The statements were made while the parties acted on the mistaken assumption that the tenant remained a tenant.
The former landlord claimed possession based on the resulting order.
issues.conclusion: The statements did not estop the successor from asserting the tenant's statutory ownership. Even assuming the tenant relinquished his right, the former landlord was not entitled to recover possession on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: A measure of agrarian reform cannot be defeated by an estoppel founded on a tenant's statement made in ignorance of legally protected rights. Further, under Sections 15 and 32P of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, even an assumed relinquishment would not restore possession to the former landlord in the circumstances; the land would be at the disposal of the Collector, and the landlord could not recover it without satisfying the applicable statutory requirements.

predicates.agrarian_tenancy_possession_case: The dispute concerns possession of agricultural land in a statutory tenancy setting.
predicates.tenant_already_owned_land: The tenant had acquired ownership of the land before making the statement.
predicates.tenant_agreed_to_surrender_under_mistake: The tenant agreed to give up possession while mistakenly believing that the former landlord remained entitled to it.

issues.definition: In a statutory tenancy possession dispute, when the tenant already owns the land and agrees to surrender it under a mistaken belief, the statement does not estop the successor or restore possession to the former landlord.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee from a person who no longer owns the land acquires no title, and possession taken under a void order may be recovered by the statutory owner's successor.
material_facts: The tenant had become the statutory owner before the purported landlord sought possession.
A possession order was made on the mistaken basis that the tenant remained a tenant liable to pay rent.
The purported landlord then sold the land to transferees, who relied on that sale and order to claim ownership and retain possession.
The tenant's successor sought restoration of possession, and the authorities found that the transferees had acquired no title.
issues.conclusion: The transferees acquired no title through the purported landlord, and the direction restoring possession to the statutory owner's successor was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 32, 14, 29, and 84 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, support the result: once the tenant became the statutory owner, no landlord-tenant relationship remained on which a landlord could base a possession proceeding for rent default. A sale by a person without title could convey no title, and possession taken under a wholly void order could be challenged and restored in the statutory recovery proceeding.

predicates.transferor_had_no_title: The person who purported to transfer the land no longer had ownership title.
